overview: A two-page State Department file register for decimal file 894A.628, “Fisheries—Taiwan,” listing correspondence from August 1932 through April 1933 concerning incursions into Philippine territorial waters by fishing vessels registered in Japanese-ruled Taiwan. The entries trace exchanges among the U.S. Consulate at Taihoku, the Department of State, the War Department, the Governor-General of the Philippine Islands, the U.S. Embassy in Japan, and the Government-General of Taiwan, including efforts to clarify or correct fisheries regulations and the stated northern boundary of the Philippines.

subfiles.title: List of papers concerning Taiwanese fishing vessels in Philippine waters
subfiles.about: This register inventories 1932–1933 correspondence about alleged violations of Philippine territorial waters by fishing vessels registered in Taiwan and the Taiwanese authorities’ regulatory response.
subfiles.summary: The first page records correspondence beginning with Ketcham’s report of August 19, 1932, stating that new Taiwan Government regulations were expected to prevent further incursions into Philippine waters. Subsequent entries document exchanges among the War Department, State Department, Governor-General of the Philippine Islands, Consulate at Taihoku, and Embassy in Japan, followed by consultations with Taiwanese industrial and fisheries officials. The continuation page records an April 1933 communication and a War Department acknowledgment concerning correction of General Order No. 33 and the northern boundary of the Philippine Islands. Some wording on page 2 is visibly garbled by OCR, but the register’s central subject remains clear.

interest: The register offers a compact chronology of a colonial-era maritime dispute involving Japanese-ruled Taiwan and the U.S.-administered Philippines. It is useful for tracing how local fishing incursions moved through consular, military, diplomatic, and colonial-government channels, and it identifies relevant orders, dates, and document numbers for locating the underlying correspondence. It also shows fisheries regulation functioning as an instrument of maritime-border enforcement in the western Pacific before the Second World War.
